awd_titl_txt: Support for Student Participation in the 2025 Modeling, Estimation, and Control Conference (MECC 2025); Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; 5-8 October 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
This grant provides funding to support student participation in the 2025 Modeling, Estimation, and Control Conference (MECC 2025), which will be held 5-8 October 2025, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. MECC is a premier conference held annually and aims to serve the scientific and engineering communities in the cross-disciplinary areas of modeling, estimation, and control of dynamical systems. It will provide a platform for the dissemination and discussion of the state-of-the-art in dynamics and controls research and create opportunities for networking with colleagues in relevant fields. The conference features contributor sessions, invited sessions, workshops, special sessions, plenary talks, keynote speeches, student and young professional programs, industry programs, and conference awards ceremonies. Funding will empower undergraduate students with high academic potential in their early stages of research development by providing them opportunities to attend the conference and have direct conversation with researchers at the forefront of dynamical systems and control. Such early engagement is expected to help build a pipeline for future rising stars in dynamical systems and control research. The grant will also support educational activities for high school students by introducing them to the field of dynamical systems, controls, and robotics. Ultimately, this grant will help significantly expand the horizon and impact of MECC 2025 to both scientific communities and society at large.
 
Student participation support focuses on reaching out to a much-broadened student body, enabling high school, undergraduate, and early-stage graduate students with high academic potential to observe first-hand outcomes from state-of-the-art research and to develop professional networks with researchers at the forefront of their fields. Multiple events and activities will be developed as part of this grant, including: i) Outreach activities in systems, controls, and robotics offered to high school students, through collaboration with industries partners in control systems and robotics; ii) Professional networking lunches and panel sessions, where participants will be coached on building professional networks and identifying pathways for pursuing either academic or industry careers; and iii) Special poster sessions where students can present their research interests and receive personalized advice and feedback, helping them to shape their research path and enhance their technical and professional development. Participant support is expected to enhance students’ scientific, technical, and professional development. Broadening access will have a huge impact on the future development of dynamics and control community and building a positive culture for future control conferences in reaching out to a broader audience and in better connecting education, research, and technology development.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The funds from this project supported a travel assistance program to broaden student participation in the 2025 Modeling, Estimation, and Control Conference (MECC 2025), held during Oct. 5-8, 2025, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The program enabled reaching out to a much-broadened student body in their early stage of research development to participate in a premier technical conference in dynamic systems, estimation, and control, expanding the program awardees’ access to professional development opportunities and strengthening the future workforce in these fields.

A key intellectual merit of the support program was its ability to engage students at a much earlier stage of research development than the traditional population of conference attendees, who are often mid- to late-stage graduate students with established publication records. By lowering the barrier to conference participation, the program introduced promising students to cutting-edge research, encouraged early engagement with the research community, and helped establish a pipeline of future researchers and innovators in dynamic systems, modeling, estimation, and control. The support enabled undergraduate students and early-stage graduate students with strong academic potential to gain first-hand exposure to state-of-the-art research, interact with leading researchers, and began building professional networks that will benefit their future academic and professional careers.

The conference’s Dynamic Systems and Control Rising-Star Sessions and Poster Display provided valuable opportunities for students to present their research, receive constructive feedback from experts, and interact with prospective employers from both academia and industry. These activities strengthened students’ research communication skills while fostering collaborations and expanding career opportunities.

Educational sessions organized in collaboration with industrial partners (e.g., Quanser and Unitree) in control systems, robotics, and autonomous systems helped participants connect fundamental concepts in dynamics and control with real-world engineering challenges. The special session, Accelerating Innovation: Automotive Control Trends and Networking, connecting students and young professionals with engineers and researchers from General Motors, Southwest Research Institute, and Amazon. Participants learned about emerging trends in automatic control, robotics, and intelligent systems while expanding their professional networks with industry leaders. These interactions increased participants’ awareness of career opportunities beyond academia and strengthened connections between the research community and industrial practice.

Under this support program, the conference also featured a mentoring lunch involving four panelists and twenty-two students and early-career participants. Through discussions on graduate education, career development, leadership, and professional growth, participants gained valuable perspective on navigating academic and industrial career pathways in dynamic systems and control. The interactive format encouraged open dialogue, facilitated mentor-mentee relationships, and helped students develop informed and successful career plans.

Beyond supporting undergraduate and graduate participants, the project also broadened participation by engaging pre-college students. The project supported industry engagement in an educational workshop that brought high school students to MECC 2025 to participate in educational activities designed to introduce them to the fields of dynamic systems, controls, and robotics. Through interactions with university researchers, graduate students, and industry professionals, participants gained early exposure to engineering research, learned about emerging technologies, and developed a better understanding of educational and career pathways in control systems and robotics. This outreach helped inspire the next generation of STEM students while strengthening the long-term pipeline into engineering and control-related disciplines.

Overall, the travel support program successfully broadened participation in MECC 2025 by enabling students from diverse educational backgrounds and career stages to engage with the dynamic systems and controls community. By integrating technical presentations, mentoring activities, educational workshops, and industry engagement, the program promoted participation, professional development, and workforce development across multiple educational levels. The project advanced NSF’s goal of broadening participation in STEM by cultivating a diverse pipeline of future researchers and engineers to contribute to the dynamic systems, control, and robotics community.
